title: The job interview
blurb: Interview language, and the CV that gets you in the room

Stage 3 · Grammar

Answering the five questions

Almost every interview in English asks these. The shape of the answer matters more than the words.

Read four answers Danielle gives in the recording.
  • I’ve worked as a sports journalist for six years.
  • I’d really like to get into online publishing.
  • I’m good at interviewing people.
  • I find it hard to say no.
Which of these four use grammar from this unit?

One is the Present Perfect with for; one is the infinitive with to.

The five questions
They askThey want to knowStart your answer like this
What qualifications have you got?the paper: degree, diploma, certificateI’ve got a degree in… · I studied… at…
How much experience do you have?the years, and whereI’ve worked as a… for… · My first job was… · I’m currently…
Why do you want this job?that you chose them, not just any jobI enjoy my present job, but… · I’d really like to…
What are your strengths and weaknesses?that you know yourselfI’m good at… · I can… when I need to · I find it hard to…, but I’m working on that
What’s your greatest achievement?one story, with a resultTwo years ago I… · I won… · I was quite pleased.
Do you have any questions?Always say yes. Yes, I do have a few actually… — then ask about the team, the first six months, or what success looks like.
Present Perfect infinitive with to

THE SHAPE. Answer, then one example, then stop. Two sentences beat five.

THE WEAKNESS. Name a real one, then add what you do about it: …but I’m working on that.

THE GRAMMAR. for / since for how long, and to + verb for what you want.

Not “I work there since six years”, not “I have no weaknesses”, not “No, I don’t have any questions.”

This is the last language of the level. Everything in it has been taught already.

THE SHAPE OF A GOOD ANSWER. Answer the question in one sentence, give one concrete example, then stop. Danielle does this every time: I’ve worked as a sports journalist for six years. My first job was working for a local newspaper in my town. Two sentences. She does not explain her whole life.

EXPERIENCE. This is where the Present Perfect earns its place. I’ve worked as a… for six years tells them you are still doing it. I worked there for two years tells them that job is finished. Danielle uses both in the same answer, and the interviewer hears the difference.

WHY THIS JOB. Never criticise your present employer. Use Danielle’s move: say something good, then say what you want. I enjoy my present job, but I’d really like to get into online publishing.

STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES. Give two or three strengths with I’m good at… and I can… Then give one real weakness and finish it: I find it hard to say no sometimes… but I’m working on that. A weakness with no ending sounds like a warning; a weakness with an ending sounds honest.

Three things that lose the job: “I work there since six years” (wrong tense and wrong word) · “I don’t really have any weaknesses” · “No, I don’t have any questions.”

Every structure in this table came from an earlier unit of this level. The interview is not new language — it is the language you already have, said under pressure.

Danielle’s own words, from the recording.

Full grammar reference — Interview language

Form

Talking about experienceI’ve worked as a journalist for six years.
Talking about the presentI’m currently writing for a sports magazine.
Describing a roleMy job is to make the work visible.
Strengths and weaknessesI’m good at interviewing people. · I find it hard to say no.
Asking backCould you tell me more about the team?

When and why we use it

  • Answer in three moves: the fact, one example, and what it means for this job.
  • Use the Present Perfect for the whole career, and the Past Simple for one particular job.
  • A good weakness answer has two parts: the weakness, and what you are doing about it.
  • Always have one question ready — it shows you have thought about the company.

Signal words

currently · previously · for / since · I’d say · for example

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I work here since 2019. → I have worked here since 2019.Still true now.
  • I have no weaknesses. → I find it hard to say no, so I’m learning to…An honest answer with a solution.
  • I am working there for six years. → I have been working there for six years.Started in the past, still true.
  • My job is make reports. → My job is to make reports.Infinitive with to.

Don’t confuse it with

I’ve worked (career, up to now) against I worked (one finished job). Interviewers listen for this.

Stage 6 · The model

The CV that got her the interview

Read it as a writer, not as a reader. You are going to copy its shape.

Danielle Moreau

Sports journalist · Montreal, Canada · d.moreau@example.com · +1 514 555 0148

PERSONAL PROFILE
A motivated sports journalist with six years’ experience in newspaper, magazine and online writing. Confident interviewer, comfortable working to a deadline, and a genuine team player. Currently looking to move into online publishing.

WORK EXPERIENCE

Writing two feature articles a week on ice hockey. My main role is to interview players and coaches and to turn those interviews into features.

Stage 7 · Now you

Now you

Write the CV, then sit the interview.

Useful language

Interviewer — Take a seat. · Tell me about yourself. · What qualifications have you got? · How much experience do you have? · Why do you want this job? · What are your strengths and weaknesses? · What’s your greatest achievement? · Do you have any questions?

Candidate — I’ve got a degree in… · I’ve worked as a… for… · I’m currently… · I’d really like to… · I’m good at… · I find it hard to…, but I’m working on that. · Yes, I do have a few actually…

CV — Personal profile · Work experience · Education · Skills · Achievements · References: available on request.

1 · Write your own CV. Use Danielle’s six sections and her phrases.

Real or invented, but keep it consistent — you will be interviewed on it in a moment.

  • Personal profile — three lines. Start with an adjective: A motivated… / A confident… Include how long, and what you want next.
  • Work experience — newest first. Each one: job title, place, years. Then one line with My main role is/was to…
  • Education — what, where, when.
  • Skills — a list. Languages first. No sentences.
  • Achievements — one line, with a year.
  • References — Available on request.
2 · Work in pairs. Student A is the interviewer, Student B is the candidate.

The candidate answers from their own CV. The interviewer asks the five questions and one of their own.

Card A — interviewer

You are head of HR. Your goal: find out whether this person can actually do the job, and whether they chose you or just any job. Ask the five questions in order. Ask one follow-up on the weakest answer. Finish with “Do you have any questions?”

Card B — candidate

You are you, from the CV you just wrote. Your goal: get to a second interview. Answer in two sentences each, never one word. Say how long with for or since. Have two real questions ready for the end.

Run it once, then swap roles and run it again with the other person’s CV. The second run is the one that counts.

Feedback
2 · Your teacher is the interviewer. You are the candidate.

Answer from the CV you just wrote. Your teacher asks the five questions and one of their own.

Card A — your teacher is the interviewer

Head of HR. Goal: find out whether this person can actually do the job, and whether they chose you or just any job. Five questions in order, one follow-up on the weakest answer, then “Do you have any questions?”

Card B — you are the candidate

You are you, from the CV you just wrote. Goal: get to a second interview. Two sentences per answer, never one word. Say how long with for or since. Have two real questions ready for the end.

Run it once, then swap roles — you interview your teacher. The second run is the one that counts.

Feedback
2 · Answer the five questions out loud, from your CV.

Record yourself if you can. Two sentences per answer, never one word. Then play it back and check three things: did you say for or since correctly, did you finish the weakness, and did you have a question at the end?
